paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant, learned AGA and
perused the record.

Learned counsel for the applicant, in the light of the said
allegations, argues that no recovery was affected from the
applicant and the applicant was linked with the offence in
question solely based upon the statement of the co-accused
which is not admissible in evidence in view of the law as
explained in the case of Tofan Singh v. State of Tamil Nadu -
(2021) 4 SCC 1. It is further argued that one of the co-accused
from whom the recovery was affected has been enlarged on bail
vide order dated 11.01.2024. As regards the criminal
antecedents, it is argued that the applicant was linked with the
offences stated in Para 25(d), (e), (f), (g) & (h) in which he is on
bail.

learned AGA, on the other hand, opposes the bail application
by arguing that the recovery as shown in the FIR is more than
commercial quantity, as such, the tests of Section 37 of NDPS
Act has to be satisfied and looking into the criminal antecedents
of the applicant, the bail application should be rejected. He,
however, does not deny that the co-accused from whom
recovery was made was enlarged on bail and the said order is
not under challenge.

The scope of Section 37 of NDPS Act came up for
consideration before the Supreme Court in Mohd Muslim @
Hussain v. State (NCT of Delhi); 2023 LiveLaw (SC) 260
wherein, interpreting Section 37, the Supreme Court observed
as under: 
"18. The conditions which courts have to be cognizant of are that there are
reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is "not guilty of such
offence" and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
What is meant by "not guilty" when all the evidence is not before the
court? It can only be a prima facie determination. That places the court's
discretion within a very narrow margin. Given the mandate of the general
law on bails (Sections 436, 437 and 439, CrPC) which classify offences
based on their gravity, and instruct that certain serious crimes have to be
dealt with differently while considering bail applications, the additional
condition that the court should be satisfied that the accused (who is in law
presumed to be innocent) is not guilty, has to be interpreted reasonably.
Further the classification of offences under Special Acts (NDPS Act, etc.),
which apply over and above the ordinary bail conditions required to be
assessed by courts, require that the court records its satisfaction that the
accused might not be guilty of the offence and that upon release, they are
not likely to commit any offence. These two conditions have the effect of
overshadowing other conditions. In cases where bail is sought, the court
assesses the material on record such as the nature of the offence,
likelihood of the accused co-operating with the investigation, not fleeing
from justice: even in serious offences like murder, kidnapping, rape, etc.
On the other hand, the court in these cases under such special Acts, have
to address itself principally on two facts: likely guilt of the accused and
the likelihood of them not committing any offence upon release. This court

has generally upheld such conditions on the ground that liberty of such
citizens have to - in cases when accused of offences enacted under special
laws – be balanced against the public interest.

Considering the fact that the co-accused has been enlarged
on bail and no recovery was affected from the applicant, the
applicant is entitled to be enlarged on bail. In view thereof, the
application is allowed.

evidence.

of the Act was considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in

following effect (paragraphs 18, 19 and 20) :- 
"18. The conditions which courts have to be cognizant of

Given the mandate of the general law on bails (Sections
436, 437 and 439, CrPC) which classify offences based

be satisfied that the accused (who is in law presumed to

reasonably. Further the classification of offences under

above the ordinary bail conditions required to be

sought, the court assesses the material on record such as
the nature of the offence, likelihood of the accused co-
operating with the investigation, not fleeing from justice:
even in serious offences like murder, kidnapping, rape,

liberty of such citizens have to - in cases when accused

Learned AGA opposes the bail application by arguing that as
the recovery was more than the commercial quantity, as such,
the test of Section 37 is to be satisfied. He argues that the
applicant has the criminal antecedents of one case under Cow
Slaughter Act, however he admits that he has no criminal
antecedents of an offence under the NDPS Act.

Considering the submissions made at the bar, it is clear that
the test of Section 37 has to be satisfied. Section 37 of the Act
came up for interpretation before the Supreme Court in the case
of Mohd. Muslim @ Hussain vs. State (NCT of Delhi) 2023
Live Law (SC) 260 wherein the Supreme Court has held as
under :
"18. The conditions which courts have to be cognizant of are
that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused
is "not guilty of such offence" and that he is not likely to
commit any offence while on bail. What is meant by "not guilty"

when all the evidence is not before the court? It can only be a
prima facie determination. That places the court's discretion
within a very narrow margin. Given the mandate of the general
law on bails (Sections 436, 437 and 439, CrPC) which classify
offences based on their gravity, and instruct that certain serious
crimes have to be dealt with differently while considering bail
applications, the additional condition that the court should be
satisfied that the accused (who is in law presumed to be
innocent) is not guilty, has to be interpreted reasonably.
Further the classification of offences under Special Acts (NDPS
Act, etc.), which apply over and above the ordinary bail
conditions required to be assessed by courts, require that the
court records its satisfaction that the accused might not be
guilty of the offence and that upon release, they are not likely to
commit any offence. These two conditions have the effect of
overshadowing other conditions. In cases where bail is sought,
the court assesses the material on record such as the nature of
the offence, likelihood of the accused co-operating with the
investigation, not fleeing from justice: even in serious offences
like murder, kidnapping, rape, etc. On the other hand, the court
in these cases under such special Acts, have to address itself
principally on two facts: likely guilt of the accused and the
likelihood of them not committing any offence upon release.
This court has generally upheld such conditions on the ground
that liberty of such citizens have to - in cases when accused of
offences enacted under special laws – be balanced against the

As the applicant has no criminal antecedents of an offence

condition also stands satisfied in favour of the applicant.

entitled for the bail. The bail application is allowed.

Heard learned counsel for the applicant as well as learned

Learned counsel for the applicant argued that no recovery
was effected from the applicant. He further argued that even in
investigation, the applicant was not assigned the role of firing.
He draws my attention to the C.D.-56 in which it was observed
that the recovery of bullets was the sole basis based upon

which, the applicant was linked with the offence as in another
case, a pistol was recovered from the applicant in Case Crime
No.195 of 2019 and the bullets allegedly used for the
commission of the present offence, could be that of the weapon
which was recovered from the applicant and based upon the
said alone, the applicant was linked with the offence in
question.

Learned A.G.A. on the other hand, strongly opposed the
prayer for bail by arguing that the criminal history of the
applicant demonstrates that the applicant has misused the
liberty of bail on each occasion in which he was enlarged on
bail and the applicant has also been convicted of an offence
under Section 302 I.P.C. and considering these facts, the present

bail application should be rejected.

Considering the submissions made at the bar, prima facie two
persons were said to have committed the offence in question.
Subsequently, the applicant was linked with the offence based
upon the recovery of the bullets and the pistol recovered from
the applicant in which similar bullets were used.

It is argued by the learned counsel for the applicant that in
the F.I.R., there was no mention of five persons. Thus, the basic

title: BAIL No. 201600026032024 — Allahabad High Court, 09 Apr 2024 (Judge: PANKAJ BHATIA)

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant as well as learned
A.G.A. and perused the record.

Learned A.G.A. vehemently opposed the bail prayer by arguing
that as huge quantities of pharmaceutical products were
recovered without any explanation and corroboration of the
bills, the applicant was linked with the offence in question. He
places reliance on Section 80 of the NDPS Act and argues that
the prosecution can simultaneously prosecute the applicant
under both the Act. He further argues that as the quantity
recovered was above the commercial quantity, the test of
Section 37 of the NDPS Act has to be satisfied.

In the light of the rival contentions, as allegedly the goods
seized were having more than the commercial quantity, the test
of Section 37 of the NDPS Act has to be satisfied. True import
of section 37 was considered by the Supremem Court in the
case of Mohd Muslim @ Hussain vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
reported in 2023 Live Law (SC) 260, to the following effect
(paragraphs 18, 19 and 20) :-
"18. The conditions which courts have to be cognizant of are
that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused
is "not guilty of such offence" and that he is not likely to
commit any offence while on bail. What is meant by "not guilty"
when all the evidence is not before the court? It can only be
prima facie determination. That places the court's discretion
within a very narrow margin. Given the mandate of the general
law on bails (Sections 436, 437 and 439, CrPC) which classify
offences based on their gravity, and instruct that certain serious

3
crimes have to be dealt with differently while considering bail
applications, the additional condition that the court should be
satisfied that the accused (who is in law presumed to be
innocent) is not guilty, has to be interpreted reasonably.
Further the classification of offences under Special Acts (NDPS
Act, etc.), which apply over and above the ordinary bail
conditions required to be assessed by courts, require that the
court records its satisfaction that the accused might not be
guilty of the offence and that upon release, they are not likely to
commit any offence. These two conditions have the effect of
overshadowing other conditions. In cases where bail is sought,
the court assesses the material on record such as the nature of
the offence, likelihood of the accused co-operating with the
investigation, not fleeing from justice: even in serious offences
like murder, kidnapping, rape, etc. On the other hand, the court
in these cases under such special Acts, have to address itself
principally on two facts: likely guilt of the accused and the
likelihood of them not committing any offence upon release.
This court has generally upheld such conditions on the ground
that liberty of such citizens have to - in cases when accused of
offences enacted under special laws ? be balanced against the
public interest.

On a plain reading of Section 22 of the NDPS Act, the offence
is the contravention of any of the condition of the license being
violated by any person charged with the offence, whereas for
dealing with pharmaceutical products, no license is either

7
prescribed or necessary as such, the essential foundation for
trying the applicant under Section 22 and Section 8 of the
NDPS Act is prima facie missing in the present case. Thus, the
first condition specified under Section 37 of the NDPS Act is
clearly satisfied in the case of the applicant.

As regards the contention of learned A.G.A. that the second
shop of the applicant did not have the license under the Drugs
and Cosmetics Act can not be accepted at this stage as the same
would lead to punishment under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act
and not under the NDPS Act. The other submission of learned
A.G.A. in the light of mandate of Section 80 of the NDPS Act
that the provisions of this Act shall be in addition to and not
derogation of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act is not in question as
the allegations have to fall as an offence under NDPS Act.

In view of the reasoning as recorded above, I am of the view
that the applicant is entitled to be released on bail. Accordingly,
the bail application is allowed.

member of any gang. The applicant is in jail in this matter since

provisions of Gangster Act has been invoked against the
applicant and the material which has been made the basis of
lodging the first information report in this case is not sufficient
enough to raise a presumption that the applicant is either guilty
of the offences mentioned in the gang chart or may commit the
same offences again if the facility of bail is granted to him. It is
further submitted that co-accused of the instant case, namely,
Natthu  and Ram Kishore alias Kishori and Chunnu Lal alias

conditions/restrictions.

Heard learned counsel for the applicant and  learned 
A.G.A. for the State.

In terms of the F.I.R., it was alleged that on the basis of the
information received, a search team was constituted and on the
basis of the search carried out from the applicant allegedly 1 kg
150 gms charas was recovered.  In the light of the said

is no material to suggest  the recovery was made from the
conscious possession at the instance of the applicant. He further
argues that there are no independent witness to the search. He
further argues that in the matter in which the sample was drawn
is contrary to the notification of the year, 2022 as well as
mandate of Section 52 A of the N.D.P.S. Act. He places reliance
upon judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in  Mohd
Muslim @ Hussain v. State (NCT of Delhi); 2023 LiveLaw
(SC) 260 and Yusuf @ Asif v. State; Criminal Appeal No.3191
of 2023 decided on 13.10.2023. He lastly argues that the
applicant has no criminal antecedents under N.D.P. Act and he
is in jail since 18.12.2023.

Learned A.G.A. opposes the bail application  and
submitted that In view of the bar created by Section 37 of the
N.D.P.S. Act, the bail application is liable to be rejected. He,
however, does not disputes the fact that the applicants have no
criminal antecedents under N.D.P.S Act.

Considering the arguments raised at bar, as the alleged
recovery is more than commercial quantity, the test of Section
37 has to be satisfied. The scope of Section 37 of NDPS Act
came up for consideration before the Supreme Court in Mohd

Muslim @ Hussain v. State (NCT of Delhi); 2023 LiveLaw
(SC) 260 wherein, interpreting Section 37, the Supreme Court
observed as under: 
"18. The conditions which courts have to be cognizant of are that there are
reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is "not guilty of such
offence" and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
What is meant by "not guilty" when all the evidence is not before the
court? It can only be a prima facie determination. That places the court's
discretion within a very narrow margin. Given the mandate of the general
law on bails (Sections 436, 437 and 439, CrPC) which classify offences
based on their gravity, and instruct that certain serious crimes have to be
dealt with differently while considering bail applications, the additional
condition that the court should be satisfied that the accused (who is in law
presumed to be innocent) is not guilty, has to be interpreted reasonably.
Further the classification of offences under Special Acts (NDPS Act, etc.),
which apply over and above the ordinary bail conditions required to be
assessed by courts, require that the court records its satisfaction that the
accused might not be guilty of the offence and that upon release, they are
not likely to commit any offence. These two conditions have the effect of
overshadowing other conditions. In cases where bail is sought, the court
assesses the material on record such as the nature of the offence,
likelihood of the accused co-operating with the investigation, not fleeing
from justice: even in serious offences like murder, kidnapping, rape, etc.
On the other hand, the court in these cases under such special Acts, have
to address itself principally on two facts: likely guilt of the accused and
the likelihood of them not committing any offence upon release. This court
has generally upheld such conditions on the ground that liberty of such
citizens have to - in cases when accused of offences enacted under special
laws – be balanced against the public interest.

In the present case, prima facie, there was no independent
witness of the search, the mandate of Section 52-A has not be
followed. On these two discrepancies, prima facie view can be
formed that the prosecution may not be able to establish its case
against the applicant. It is clarified that this observation is only
for the purposes of consideration of bail and would not have
any adverse effect on trial. In respect of the second condition
specified under Section 37, as the applicant has no criminal
antecedents, in view of the law as laid down in the case of
Ranjitsing Brahmajeetsingh Sharma Vs. State of
Maharashtra & Anr: AIR 2005 Sc 2277, the second set of
Section 37 is also satisfied in the case of the applicant.

In view of the reason recorded as above, the applicant is
enlarged on bail. Accordingly, the bail application is allowed.

title: BAIL No. 201600019662024 — Allahabad High Court, 23 Feb 2024 (Judge: SUBHASH VIDYARTHI)

paragraphs.text:
Heard Sri Anil Kumar Tiwari, learned counsel for the
applicant, Sri Amitabh Chaturvedi, the learned A.G.A. for the
State and perused the records.

The aforesaid case has been registered on the basis of an
F.I.R. lodged on 01.05.2022 against the applicant and one
Gokaran @ Karan @ Sonu Nishad, stating that the accused
persons were riding on a motorcycle, which was intercepted
during a routine checking by the police party, and the accused
persons fired a shot towards the police party. Police also fired
shots, in which both the accused persons received gun shot
injuries. As per the FIR version, one pistol each was recovered
from each of the accused persons and some other articles were
also recovered, which the accused persons confessed to have
been stolen or robbed by them. The FIR mentions that no
independent person has witnessed the recovery.

In the affidavit filed in support of bail application, it has been
stated that prior to his arrest, the applicant was involved in two
cases in both of the cases, the applicant has already been
granted bail. After his arrest, the applicant has been implicated
in as many as 21 cases on the basis of same recovery. The
applicant has already been granted bail in six cases in which he
has been implicated after his arrest. It has also been submitted
on behalf of the applicant that the co-accused Gokaran has
already been enlarged on bail by this court by means of an order
dated 07.08.2023 in Criminal Misc. Bail Application No.9862
of 2023.

The learned A.G.A. has opposed the prayer for bail but he
could not dispute the aforesaid aspects of the matter.

Having considered the aforesaid facts and circumstances of
the case and keeping in view the fact that the recovery was not
witnessed by any independent person; that the applicant has
been implicated in 21 cases on the basis of same recovery out of
which he has already been granted bail in six cases; that the
applicant is languishing in jail since 01.05.2022 and without
making any observation, which may affect the merits of the
case, I am of the view that the aforesaid facts are sufficient for
making out a case for enlargement of the applicant on bail in
the aforesaid crime.
Accordingly, this bail application stands allowed.

the applicant has been involved in this case  without there being
any material or evidence against him.

committed suicide in the house of the applicant and other co-
accused persons where she was working as a housemate and
without there being any material only on the basis of
apprehension allegations have been levelled that she has been
subjected to sexual assault and it is on this score she has
committed suicide.

While drawing attention of this Court towards the
postmortem report of the deceased, it is submitted that except a
ligature mark  no injury of any other kind has been found on the
body of the deceased belying the story as cooked up by the
prosecution.

It is further submitted that though the material prosecution
witnesses whose statements were recorded by the Investigating
Officer  have levelled allegations against the applicant and other
co-accused  persons during the course of investigation but they

title: BAIL No. 201600018132024 — Allahabad High Court, 09 Jul 2024 (Judge: PANKAJ BHATIA)

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant and
learned A.G.A. for the  and perused the record.

The accused-applicant seeks bail in Case
Crime No.08 of 2024 under sections 8/22 of
N.D.P.S. Act, Police Station Tikonia, District
Lakhimpur Kheri.

Learned counsel for the applicant has argued
that the recovery of the alleged substance was not
effected in accordance with law.  There were no
independent witnesses to the search.  It is further
argued that the mandate of Section 52-A as well
as two standing orders were not followed.   He
lastly argued that the applicant  is in custody since
14.1.2024 having no criminal history of an offence
under the N.D.P.S. Act or any other offence, hence,
the  applicant may be enlarged on bail.

Learned A.G.A. opposed the prayer for bail by
arguing that the recovery is more than the

commercial quantity, which is 110 grams in the
case of Alprazolam, as such the bail application
has to be rejected.

Hon'ble Supreme Court had the occasion to
deal with the aspect of Section 37 and the
conditions prescribed therein in the case of Mohd
Muslim @ Hussain vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
reported in 2023 Live Law (SC) 260.  While
dealing with the scope of Section 37, Hon'ble Apex
Court observed as under:- 
"18. The conditions which courts have to be cognizant of
are that there are reasonable grounds for believing that
the accused is "not guilty of such offence" and that he is
not likely to commit any offence while on bail. What is
meant by "not guilty" when all the evidence is not before
the court? It can only be prima facie determination. That
places the court's discretion within a very narrow margin.
Given the mandate of the general law on bails (Sections
436, 437 and 439, CrPC) which classify offences based on
their gravity, and instruct that certain serious crimes have
to be dealt with differently while considering bail
applications, the additional condition that the court should
be satisfied that the accused (who is in law presumed to
be innocent) is not guilty, has to be interpreted reasonably.
Further the classification of offences under Special Acts
(NDPS Act, etc.), which apply over and above the ordinary
bail conditions required to be assessed by courts, require
that the court records its satisfaction that the accused
might not be guilty of the offence and that upon release,
they are not likely to commit any offence. These two

conditions have the effect of overshadowing other
conditions. In cases where bail is sought, the court
assesses the material on record such as the nature of the
offence, likelihood of the accused co-operating with the
investigation, not fleeing from justice: even in serious
offences like murder, kidnapping, rape, etc. On the other
hand, the court in these cases under such special Acts,
have to address itself principally on two facts: likely guilt of
the accused and the likelihood of them not committing any
offence upon release. This court has generally upheld such
conditions on the ground that liberty of such citizens have
to - in cases when accused of offences enacted under
special laws – be balanced against the public interest.
Thus, the bail application is allowed.

Heard learned counsel for the applicant and Sri S.M. Singh

applicant (Gaurav Mishra) is languishing in jail since

8/22/27A/29 of Narcotic Drugs & Psychotropic Substances Act,
challaned by Central Bureau of Narcotics, Mahanagar,
Lucknow, District-Lucknow.

Learned counsel for the applicant has submitted that the
present applicant has been falsely implicated in the present case
as he has not committed any offence as alleged in the
prosecution story.

As per the prosecution story so narrated in the Panchnama/
Recovery Memo on 08.09.2023 at about 8:00 P.M., a secret
information was received in the office of Deputy Narcotics
Commissioner, Lucknow, which was reduced in writing on a
prescribed format CBN-1, which is annexed as Annexure
No.C.A.-1 of the counter affidavit. As per the information on
08.09.2023, a large consignment of NRX drugs i.e. Alprazolam,
Tramadol & Buprenorphine tablets, were without bills and
necessary documents were under shipment from Rajasthan to
Lucknow through Trackon Courier Service having Docket
No.500281308647 in the name of a fake medical firm.

Learned counsel has further submitted that the present
applicant is an innocent person. He has no concern with the
present offence. The applicant has been falsely implicated in
this case on the basis of confession of co-accused person before
the NCB officers, there is no evidentiary value of the statement
allegedly recorded by the officers of the raiding team, as the
same is barred by Article 20 (3) of the Constitution of India,
prima facie, no case is made out against the applicant to dis-
entitle him for grant of the bail in view of the provisions of
sections 37 of the NDPS Act. Further, co-accused Kunal Gupta,
having similar role, has been enlarged on bail by this Court vide
order dated 29.05.2024 passed in Criminal Misc. Bail
Application No.15278 of 2023, the another co-accused, namely,
Abhishek Mishra has also been granted bail by this Court vide
order dated 30.05.2024 passed in Criminal Misc. Bail
Application No.468 of 2024, therefore, on the basis of
principles of party, the present applicant may also be enlarged
on bail. The applicant undertakes that he shall cooperate in the
trial proceedings and shall not misuse the liberty of bail, if
granted by this Court and shall abide by all terms and
conditions of the bail order.

Learned counsel for the applicant has further submitted that
there is no previous criminal history of any kind whatsoever
against the present applicant. Therefore, learned counsel for the
applicant has stated that in the present case, the present
applicant has been implicated only on the basis of confessional
statement of the co-accused recorded under Section 67 of
NDPS Act, which is not admissible in the trial, in view of law
laid down by the Apex Court in re; Tofan Singh Vs. State of
Tamil Nadu, (2013) 16 SCC 31.

paragraphs.text: Heard learned counsel for the applicant, learned AGA and perused the record.

Learned AGA for the State opposes the bail application by arguing that the test of
Section 19(4)(b) of the Act, 1986 has to be satisfied before the Court, the applicant
can be enlarged on bail. She further argues that the cases against the applicant
reflected in the gang chart would fall within the scope of 'public order' and would
not be a case of mere 'law and order' problem as criminal acts per se affect the
conscience of the society at large and thus, the bail application of the applicant
should be rejected, more so in view of the criminal history of the applicant.

The scope of Section 19(4)(b) of the said Act was also considered in the said
case placing reliance on the judgement of the Supreme Court interpreting a similar
provision in the case of Mohd. Muslim @ Hussain vs. State (NCT of Delhi), 2023

LiveLaw (SC) 260. Following the mandate of the said order and the reasoning
contained therein, prima facie in respect of the first test prescribed under Section
19(4)(b) of the Act, 1986, a prima facie case is made in favour of the applicant.

Considering the fact that the allegations would not fall within the scope of
'public order' and are simple law and order problems further as, there is no material
to suggest that the applicant would indulge in a similar offence on being enlarged
on bail, the second of the said test is also satisfied in favour of the applicant. On the
consideration recorded above, the applicant is entitled to be enlarged on bail. In
view thereof, the application is allowed.

title: BAIL No. 201600011322024 — Allahabad High Court, 04 Apr 2024 (Judge: PANKAJ BHATIA)

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant and
Shri S.M. Singh Royekwar, learned counsel for the 
and perused the record.

The accused-applicant seeks bail in Case
Crime No.0192 of 2023 under sections 8/20 of
N.D.P.S. Act, Police Station - Bazar Shukul, District
Amethi.

Learned counsel for the applicant argued that
the statement of the co accused under Section 67
of the N.D.P.S. is not admissible in the light of the
law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the
case of  Tofan Singh Vs. State of Tamilnadu :
AIR 2020 SC 5592.  It is further argued that 

there is no material to link the applicant with the
offence in question.   The applicant is languishing
in jail since 19.10.2023, hence he may be released
on bail.

Learned A.G.A. argued that a very huge
quantity of  of ganja was recovered from the
vehicle in question and the persons had taken the
name of the applicant, thus the applicant was
directly connected with the offence in question.  
As the recovery is more than the commercial
quantity, as such the test of Section 37 of the
N.D.P.S. has to be satisfied before the bail is
granted, as such the application for bail  should be
rejected.  Learned A.G.A. however agreed that the
applicant has no criminal history.

The true intent and interpretation of Section
37 of the Act was considered by Hon'ble Supreme
Court in the case of Mohd Muslim @ Hussain
vs. State (NCT of Delhi) reported in 2023
Live Law (SC) 260, to the following effect
(paragraphs 18, 19 and 20) :- 
"18. The conditions which courts have to be cognizant of
are that there are reasonable grounds for believing that
the accused is "not guilty of such offence" and that he is
not likely to commit any offence while on bail. What is
meant by "not guilty" when all the evidence is not before
the court? It can only be prima facie determination. That
places the court's discretion within a very narrow margin.
Given the mandate of the general law on bails (Sections

436, 437 and 439, CrPC) which classify offences based on
their gravity, and instruct that certain serious crimes have
to be dealt with differently while considering bail
applications, the additional condition that the court should
be satisfied that the accused (who is in law presumed to
be innocent) is not guilty, has to be interpreted reasonably.
Further the classification of offences under Special Acts
(NDPS Act, etc.), which apply over and above the ordinary
bail conditions required to be assessed by courts, require
that the court records its satisfaction that the accused
might not be guilty of the offence and that upon release,
they are not likely to commit any offence. These two
conditions have the effect of overshadowing other
conditions. In cases where bail is sought, the court
assesses the material on record such as the nature of the
offence, likelihood of the accused co-operating with the
investigation, not fleeing from justice: even in serious
offences like murder, kidnapping, rape, etc. On the other
hand, the court in these cases under such special Acts,
have to address itself principally on two facts: likely guilt of
the accused and the likelihood of them not committing any
offence upon release. This court has generally upheld such
conditions on the ground that liberty of such citizens have
to - in cases when accused of offences enacted under
special laws – be balanced against the public interest.

As regards the statement under Section 67
which is heavily relied upon by the learned counsel
for the respondent, it is well settled that the
statement under Section 67 is not admissible
piece of evidence  in view of the law laid down  by
Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Tofan
Singh Vs. State of Tamilnadu : AIR 2020 SC
5592.   Prima facie, there is no material to link the
applicant  with the offence in question.  As such a
reasonable view can be formed that solely based
upon the statement under Section  67 of the
N.D.P.S. Act, the prosecution  may not be able to
establish the offence under the N.D.P.S. Act
against the applicant.  As such the first of the twin
test prescribed under the N.D.P.S.Act stands
satisfied in favour of the applicant.

Heard learned counsel for the applicant as well as learned
A.G.A. and perused the record. No one appeared on behalf of
opposite party no.2 despite service of notice.

In the light of said allegations, learned counsel for the
applicant draws my attention to the medical on record, wherein
the victim has herself stated before the medical authorities that,
she was taken on a motorcycle and was administered food as a
result whereof she slept and after she woke up she saw that she
was lying outside the village. Medical on record also does not
corroborate any allegations of wrong doing on the victim. The
tentative age of the victim as per the FIR is 17 years. Thus in

view of the said facts, learned counsel for the applicants argues
that the applicants who have no criminal history and are in
custody since 05.09.2023 may be enlarged on bail.

Learned A.G.A. strongly opposes the bail application by
arguing that the date of birth of the victim, as per the school
records is 10.03.2009, as such considering the age of the victim,
the bail application deserves to be rejected.

Considering the submissions made at the bar, prima facie,
considering the allegations made in the FIR and in the
statements of the victim recorded under Sections 161 and 164
CrPC as well as her statement made before medical authorities,
there was no averment with regard to any wrong being
committed on the victim, the same is also not corroborated by
the medical on record. As regards the age, the informant herself
has disclosed the age as 17 years, whereas the document relied
upon by the learned AGA points out the age of the victim at
around 14 years, thus there is no definite document to
conclusively form any opinion with regard to the age of the
victim at this stage.

Considering the fact that allegations under Section 376 or
307 IPC are neither corroborated by any material nor have they
been specifically stated against the applicants, therefore the
applicants who have no criminal antecedents and are in custody
since 05.09.2023, deserve to be released on bail. Accordingly,
the bail application is allowed.

Let the applicant Anil Kumar be released on bail in the
abovesaid first information report number on his furnishing
personal bonds and two reliable sureties of Rs.20,000/- each to
the satisfaction of the court concerned with the following
conditions: 
(a) The applicant shall execute a bond to undertake to attend the
hearings; 
(b) The applicant shall not commit any offence similar to the
offence of which he is accused or suspected of the commission;
and 
(c) The applicant shall not directly or indirectly make any
inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the
facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such
facts to the Court or to any police officer or tamper with the
evidence.

title: BAIL No. 201600008962024 — Allahabad High Court, 30 Jan 2024 (Judge: MOHD. FAIZ ALAM KHAN)

paragraphs.text:
Learned A.G.A. informs that he has procured complete
instructions in the matter including up-to-date case diary and
the charge-sheet in this case has already been submitted.

Heard learned counsel for the accused-applicant as well as
learned A.G.A. for the State and perused the record.

Learned counsel for the accused-applicant while pressing the
bail application submits that it is a case of false implication.
The FIR of this case has been lodged against unknown persons
as it was found that some abandoned spurious countrymade
liquor was found at a place. However, during the course of the
investigation, it was found that the applicant was involved in
manufacturing and supplying of spurious liquor and thus, the
liquor and the bottles of liquor recovered were supplied by the
applicant in connivance with the other co-accused persons.

It is vehemently submitted that the case of the prosecution is
based on the confessional statement of the applicant as well as
the confessional statement of the other co-accused persons and
apart from that, there is no independent witness or evidence
which may connect the applicant with the crime.

It is further submitted that identically placed co-accused
persons, namely, Pravin Singh @ Ketan Singh and Arshad @
Shanu have been granted bail by a co-ordinate Bench of this
Court, vide orders dated 19.10.2023 and 18.9.2023 passed in
Criminal Misc. Bail Application Nos. 12577 of 2023 and 8219
of 2023 respectively and the other co-accused persons namely,
Harshendra Singh @ Raja, Vinay Jaiswal Dheerendra Singh,
Ram Pratap Yadav and Sandip Jaiswal have been granted bail
by the trial court vide orders dated 5.10.2023, 21.10.2023,
30.10.2023, 24.8.2023 and 5.12.2023 passed in bail application
Nos. 3344 of 2023, 3560 of 2023, 3627 of 2023, 2954 of 2023
and 4000 of 2023, respectively.

It is further submitted that the criminal history of the
applicant has been adequately explained the supplementary
affidavit dated 19.1.2024. The applicant is languishing in jail in
this case since 28.4.2022. Charge sheet in this case has already
been filed and there is no apprehension that after being released
on bail he may flee from the course of law or may otherwise
misuse the liberty.

title: BAIL No. 201600008692024 — Allahabad High Court, 01 Feb 2024 (Judge: KARUNESH SINGH PAWAR)

paragraphs.text:
Heard Sri Arun Sinha, learned counsel for the applicant, Sri
Mahesh Kumar and Sri Sanjeev Kumar Dwivedi, learned
counsel for the complainant, learned A.G.A. for the State and
perused the record.

Learned counsel for applicant submits that informant is not
an eye witness. Incident has been narrated by Shubham Verma.
The named accused persons Vaseer Khan and Jalaluddin have
been enlarged on bail by this Court vide orders dated
05.01.2024 & 18.01.2024 passed in Criminal Misc. Bail
Application Nos.13143 of 2023 & 15248 of 2023. He submits
that apart from the above named two co-accused persons, co-
accused Manoj Yadav and Manish Yadav alias Kallu who were

not named in the F.I.R. have also been enlarged on bail by this
Court as well as Co-ordinate Bench of this Court vide orders
dated 08.01.2024 & 06.12.2023 passed in Criminal Misc. Bail
Application Nos.10378 of 2023 & 12350 of 2023. 
It is contended on behalf of the applicant that there is absolutely
no material against the applicant except the information given
by a secret informer on parcha No.1 of the case diary that in the
influence of the applicant Rahul Yadav commits the criminal
activity. He submits that his case is on better footing than the 
named accused persons namely, Jalaluddin and Vaseer Khan.
The applicant is in jail since 04.03.2023.

Learned A.G.A. as well as learned counsel for the
complainant have opposed the bail prayer. They have submitted
that applicant has criminal history of 17 cases and, therefore, he
is not entitled to be enlarged on bail.

Rebutting the aforesaid, learned counsel for the applicant
submits that he has explained the criminal history in para 47 of
the bail application. He is on bail in all the 17 cases. He submits
that merely because applicant has a criminal history will not
dis-entitle him to be enlarged on bail. He has relied on
judgment of Supreme Court in the case of Maulana Mohd.
Amir Rashadi vs. State of U.P. & Anr. [Criminal Appeal
No.159 of 2012]. He submits that role of the accused in the
particular case has to be seen while granting bail, emphasis is
on para 6. He has further relied on the judgment of Supreme
Court in the case of Prabhakar Tewari vs. State of Uttar
Pradesh [AIRONLINE 2020 SC 96].

On due consideration to the submissions advanced, perusal of
the record as also the bail orders of the co-accused persons
named above who have been enlarged on bail, period of
incarceration gone into by the applicant and the explanation of
the criminal history so also the judgment of Supreme Court
passed in Maulana Mohd. Amir Rashadi & Prabhakar Tewari
(supra), prima facie, this Court is of the opinion that case of the
applicant is on better footing than the named co-accused
persons Jalaluddin and Vaseer Khan, without expressing any
opinion on merits of the case, I find it to be a fit case for
enlarging the applicant on bail.
Accordingly, the bail application is allowed.

title: BAIL No. 201600006522024 — Allahabad High Court, 16 Apr 2024 (Judge: PANKAJ BHATIA)

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant, learned AGA and
perused the record.

The accused-applicant seeks bail in Case Crime No.547 of
2023 under section 8/21 NDPS Act, P.S. Safdarganj, District
Barabanki.

In the light of the said, the contention of the counsel for the
applicant is that in terms of the arrest memo, which has been
filed as SA-I to the supplementary affidavit, the arrest was
shown at 08:45 pm on 30.11.2023 which bears the FIR number
also whereas, as per the FIR, the same was registered on
01.12.2023 at about 01:45 am, which clearly is not possible. It
is further argued that as per the FIR, the sample was drawn on
30.11.2023, however, the same was sent for analysis on
08.12.2023 as is evident from CA-5 on record. He further
argues that the mandate of Section 52-A of the NDPS Act was
not followed and he places reliance on the judgment of the
Supreme Court in the case of Yusuf @ Asif v. State; Criminal
Appeal No.3191 of 2023 decided on 13.10.2023. He further
argues that the applicant has no criminal history and is in
custody since 30.11.2023.

Learned AGA opposes the bail application by arguing that as
the recovery is more than the commercial quantity, the test of
Section 37 is be satisfied.

Considering the fact that the alleged recovery is more than
the commercial quantity which is 250 grams in the case of
morphine, the test of section 37 is to be satisfied. Section 37 of
the NDPS Act is interpreted by the Supreme Court in the case
of Mohd. Muslim @ Hussain vs. State (NCT of Delhi) 2023
Live Law (SC) 260,  to the following effect : 
"18. The conditions which courts have to be cognizant of are
that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused
is "not guilty of such offence" and that he is not likely to
commit any offence while on bail. What is meant by "not guilty"
when all the evidence is not before the court? It can only be a
prima facie determination. That places the court's discretion
within a very narrow margin. Given the mandate of the general
law on bails (Sections 436, 437 and 439, CrPC) which classify
offences based on their gravity, and instruct that certain serious
crimes have to be dealt with differently while considering bail
applications, the additional condition that the court should be
satisfied that the accused (who is in law presumed to be
innocent) is not guilty, has to be interpreted reasonably.
Further the classification of offences under Special Acts (NDPS
Act, etc.), which apply over and above the ordinary bail
conditions required to be assessed by courts, require that the
court records its satisfaction that the accused might not be
guilty of the offence and that upon release, they are not likely to
commit any offence. These two conditions have the effect of
overshadowing other conditions. In cases where bail is sought,
the court assesses the material on record such as the nature of
the offence, likelihood of the accused co-operating with the
investigation, not fleeing from justice: even in serious offences
like murder, kidnapping, rape, etc. On the other hand, the court
in these cases under such special Acts, have to address itself
principally on two facts: likely guilt of the accused and the
likelihood of them not committing any offence upon release.
This court has generally upheld such conditions on the ground
that liberty of such citizens have to - in cases when accused of
offences enacted under special laws – be balanced against the
public interest.

For all the reasons recorded above, the first test is satisfied in
favour of the applicant. As the applicant has no criminal history,
in view of the law laid down in the case of  Brahmajeetsing
Sharma vs. State of Maharashtra, (2005) 5 SCC 294 the
second of the twin condition also is found to be satisfied in
favour of the applicant. Thus, for all the reasoning recorded
above, the applicant is entitled for the bail. Thus the bail
application is allowed.

title: BAIL No. 201600005662024 — Allahabad High Court, 14 Mar 2024 (Judge: PANKAJ BHATIA)

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned for the applicant as well as
learned A.G.A. and perused the record.

Learned counsel for the applicant has argued
that the victim died on account of an accident and
the cause of death is shown as ante mortem burn
injuries.

Learned counsel for the applicant has drawn
my attention to the fact that at the time of the
inquest, the applicant was present and the
applicant has taken the deceased to the hospital
which fact is stated in Annexure No.9.   In the light
of the said, applicant argued that the applicant has
no criminal history and is languishing in jail since
20.5.2022, hence he may be released on bail.

Learned A.G.A. opposed the bail application by
arguing that the applicant is the husband of the
deceased and the cause of death as ante mortem
burn injuries and the death caused within seven
years of marriage, hence the bail application
should be rejected.

Considering the  submissions made at the bar
prima facie from the perusal of inquest report and
the statements, it is clear that the applicant had
taken the deceased to the hospital, there is no
suggestion or the document of use of any force on

the body of the deceased except the ante mortem
burn injuries coupled with the fact that there is
nothing on record to allege that soon before the
death, the applicant has subjected the deceased
to any physical or mental harassment in relation to
the demand of dowry particularly the fact that the
applicant is in custody since 20.5.2023 having no
criminal history and there is nothing on record to
demonstrate that the applicant if enlarged on bail,
would in any way adversely affect the trial and
without expressing any opinion on merit, I am of
the view that the applicant is entitled to be
released on bail.
Accordingly, the bail application is allowed.

title: BAIL No. 201600005002024 — Allahabad High Court, 10 Dec 2024 (Judge: KARUNESH SINGH PAWAR)

paragraphs.text:
It is submitted that co-accused persons namely Abhay Pratap

Singh, Ram Karan Verma, Rishabh  Singh, Kuldeep Singh,
Suravarth Singh @ Vimla Singh, Surendra Pratap Singh @
Surendar Yadav, Ravi Shankar Pandey have been granted bail
by this Court, the copies of bail order are on record.

Learned counsel for the applicant submits that previous bad
character of the applicant is irrelevant since he is not being
convicted yet in any case, therefore, the bad character or
criminal history of applicant cannot be a fact in issue hence, the
same is irrelevant for considering this bail application.

It has been further submitted that the applicant is in jail since
09.08.2023 and if facility of bail is granted, there is no
apprehension that he will flee from the judicial process and he
will abide by the orders passed by the Court below and will co-
operate in speedy trial of the case.

Learned A.G.A. as well as learned counsel for the
complainant have opposed the prayer for bail but have not
disputed the factual submissions made by the learned counsel
for the accused-applicant. Learned counsel for the complainant
has submitted that the applicant has a criminal history of several

cases.

The gang chart also prima facie appears to have been
prepared without application of mind inasmuch as Case Crime
No.77/2021 is shown in the gang chart against the applicant is
concerned. The co-accused persons namely Abhay Pratap
Singh, Ram Karan Verma, Rishabh  Singh, Kuldeep Singh,
Suravarth Singh @ Vimla Singh, Surendra Pratap Singh @
Surendar Yadav, Ravi Shankar Pandey, whose names have also

shown in the gang chart, have been granted bail and prima facie
considering the manner in which the gang chart has been
prepared de hors the U.P. Gangsters and Anti-social Activities
Rules, 2021 particularly Rule 5(iii)(a), therefore, this Court is of
the opinion that applicant may not be held guilty during trial.

Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, nature
of allegations, arguments advanced by learned counsel for the
parties, the bail orders of co-accused persons, named above,
prima facie, there appears to be non-compliance of Rule 5 (iii)
(a) of the Gangsters Act, non-application of mind in preparing
the gang chart, as discussed above, and also the twin conditions
under Section 19(4) of the Gangsters Act having been satisfied,
period of incarceration gone into by the applicant and without
expressing any opinion on the merits of the case, I find it to be a
fit case for enlarging the applicant on bail.

title: BAIL No. 201600004712024 — Allahabad High Court, 23 Jan 2024 (Judge: MOHD. FAIZ ALAM KHAN)

Station- Kunda, District- Pratapgarh, during trial, as his first
bail application is dismissed as not pressed.

Learned counsel for the accused-applicant while pressing the
bail application submits that it is a case of false implication and
all the allegations, which have been levelled by the informant as
well as the eye witnesses against the applicant and other
accused persons, are false, concocted and could not be believed.

It is further submitted that no motive has been assigned in the
F.I.R. or in the statements of the prosecution witnesses and
therefore, it is doubtful that without any motive or objective, the
death of a person may be caused.

It is also submitted that the case of the prosecution is to the
tune that on relevant day, co-accused Arun Kumar Yadav had
taken the deceased with him in his Bolero car and they were
also accompanied by the applicant and two other accused
persons, namely, Pintu Yadav @ Arvind Yadav, and Kuldeep
Yadav to a roadside restaurant and a dispute had occurred there.
Resulting in the scuffle between them and on the instigation
given by the co-accused Arun Kumar Yadav, the instant
applicant, Pintu Yadav @ Arviind Yadav and Kuldeep yadav
pushed the deceased inside a Nala (sewer), whereby he
sustained injuries and died.

Learned A.G.A., on the other hand, opposes the prayer of bail
of the applicant on the ground of heinousness of the offence,
however, he could not refute that identically placed co-accused
Pintu Yadav @ Arvind Yadav has been granted bail by a
Coordinate Bench of this Court.

title: BAIL No. 201600004652024 — Allahabad High Court, 03 Jul 2024 (Judge: KARUNESH SINGH PAWAR)

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant, learned A.G.A. for
the State as well as Sri Rajendra Pratap Singh, learned counsel
for the complainant and perused the record.

As per the prosecution case, it is alleged that pursuant to the
order  dated 15.09.2014 passed in Writ Petition No.7611/2014,
the impugned first information report was registered regarding
the forgery committed in Case No.301/2000 (Arun Kumar
Singh @ Munna vs. Kamlesh Kumar Singh) pending before the
Sub Divisional Magistrate, Kunda where allegedly the forged
file was prepared along with order dated 15.05.2001 and
consequently, mutation order dated  08.05.2012 was also
prepared.

Learned counsel for the applicant submits that after the
F.I.R., investigation was carried out and a final report was filed
by the Investigating Officer. Thereafter, one Kamlesh Kumar
Singh though not informant had filed a protest petition without
any locus which was rejected vide order dated 01.07.2017 by
the Court of Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Kunda, the

cognizance was taken and non-bailable warrants were issued
against the applicant and other co-accused persons accordingly. 
Against the order dated 01.07.2017, the co-accused Arun
Kumar Singh @ Munna and others have filed criminal revision
bearing No.171/2017 in the court of Additional Sessions Judge,
Court No.5, Pratapgarh, the Revisional Court vide order dated
02.06.2018 has set aside the order dated 01.07.2017 passed by
the learned Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Kunda and
remitted the matter back for fresh consideration. 
Against the order dated 02.06.2018 Kamlesh Kumar Singh filed
a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. bearing No.2139/2019
before this Court which was dismissed vide order dated
05.01.2023. 
After remand of the case, it was heard by the concerned court
and vide order dated 18.08.2022 final report was rejected and
learned trial court took cognizance and issued summons to the
accused persons. After coming to know the summoning order,
applicant filed a Criminal Revision before the District and
Sessions Judge, Pratapgarh which is pending. The other co-
accused Arun Kumar Singh @ Munna filed criminal revision
before the Special Judge which was rejected on 12.05.2023 and
subsequently, the same was challenged before this Court vide
Application U/S 482 No.5520/2023 which was dismissed by
this court vide order dated 21.08.2023. 
Against this order dated 21.08.2023, SLP (crl.) was filed
bearing No.14723/2023 (Arun Kumar Singh @ Munna & others
vs. State of U.P. and others) wherein the Supreme Court has
stayed the proceedings arising out of F.I.R. No.61/2015, P.S.
Kunda, District Pratapgarh. 
Learned counsel for the applicant submits that while the
applicant was in jail since 04.07.2023 in connection with Case

Crime No.444/2022, under Section 409 IPC, P.S. Raniganj,
District Pratapgarh, he was taken into custody in the present
case and he is languishing in jail since 20.07.2023. He submits
that the applicant has been granted bail in the earlier Case
Crime No.444/2022 however, in this case he is languishing in
jail since 20.07.2023. 
It is submitted on behalf of the applicant that applicant is a
government servant. No sanction has been obtained under
Section 197 Cr.P.C. The proceedings of trial have been stayed
by the Supreme Court in pending SLP (crl.). The applicant
cannot be kept behind the bars for unlimited period. 
It is lastly submitted that there is a family dispute between the
co-accused and Kamlesh Kumar Singh. Applicant is not
concerned in any manner nor he is beneficiary, and has also not
prepared any forged document. He has been falsely implicated
in this case. Offences are triable by magistrate.

Learned A.G.A. as well as learned counsel for the
complainant have opposed the bail prayer however, learned
counsel for the complainant does not dispute the fact that
proceedings are stayed. He submits that applicant is a habitual
offender and there is one more F.I.R. lodged against the
applicant and therefore, he should not be enlarged on bail.

On due consideration to the submissions advanced, perusal of
the record as also the order dated 28.11.2023 passed in SLP
(Crl.) No.14723 of 2023, period of incarceration gone into by
the applicant and the fact that offences are triable by magistrate,
without expressing any opinion on merits of the case, I find it to
be a fit case for enlarging the applicant on bail.
Accordingly, the bail application is allowed.

Learned A.G.A. strongly opposes the bail
application by arguing that the recovery was more
than the  commercial quantity as such the test of
Section 37 of the NDPS Act is to be satisfied.  Thus

on all parameters, the bail application should be
rejected.

Considering the fact that the mandate  of
Section 52-A of the NDPS Act has not been
followed as such in view of  scope  of Section 37 of
the NDPS Act as explained in the case of Mohd.
Muslim @ Hussain Vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
(Special Leave Petition (Crl.) 915 of 2023)
and the manner in which Section 37 of the NDPS
Act is to be interpreted, finding prima facie there
being non compliance of Section 52A, the first test
of the twin conditions prescribed under Section 37
is satisfied in favour of the applicants and as the
applicants have no criminal history in view of the
law as laid down in the case of Ranjitsing
Brahmajeetsing Sharma vs State Of
Maharashtra & Anr : AIR 2005 SC 2277, the
second of the twin condition as specified under
Section 37 of the NDPS Act is also satisfied in
favour of the applicant.
Thus, the bail application is allowed.

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant, Shri
Alok Kumar Singh, holding brief of Shri Sanjay
Singh Chauhan, learned counsel for the
respondent nos.2  and 3 as well as learned A.G.A.
and perused the record.

Learned counsel for the applicant argued that
no allegation of rape was made in the F.I.R. 
Subsequently, the statement of the victim "Y"  was
recorded wherein she reiterated the said version

and she stated that an attempt was made
however nothing wrong was done to them.

In the light of the said allegation, learned
counsel for the applicant argued that in the  F.I.R.,
in the statement made by victim 'Y'  under
Section  161 Cr.P.C. and in the statement before
the medical authorities, no allegation of rape was
levelled.   The medical examination also did not
record any injury on the private part.  The opinion
of the doctor that sexual violence cannot be ruled
out, prima facie contrary  to the medical findings
recorded.

Learned counsel for the applicant lastly argued
that the applicant is in custody since 28.1.2023
having criminal history of one case which has been
duly explained in bail application in which the
applicant is on bail.   Even the statement under
Section 35 (1) of the victim under the POCSO Act
has not been recorded till date as such the
applicant may be enlarged on bail looking into the
young age of the applicant.

Learned A.G.A. as well as learned counsel for
the respondent complainant have strongly
opposed the prayer for bail by arguing that in the
statement under Section 164 Cr.P.C., a specific 

allegation of rape was levelled.

What transpires from the record is that 
prima facie in terms of the F.I.R., statement under
Section 161 and the statement before the medical
authorities, no allegation of rape were levelled.  
The medical on record also does not corroborate or
points out the offence of rape.  In the statement
under Section 164 Cr.P.C., allegations of rape were
specifically levelled.   However, the victim also
stated that two boys and two girls had gone on the
same scooty.  The injury sustained by victim 'Y'
does not corroborate any allegation of rape except
for a bite mark on the neck.

injuries were caused to him which resulted in the
death of the deceased.   In the light of the said
allegation, learned counsel for the applicant draws

report indicate two incised wounds on the left side
of the head and back of the head.

learned counsel for the applicant is that the role of
catching hold was only assigned to the applicant
and the role of assaulting was assigned to one
Raju.  The applicant is in jail since 16.8.2023 and
has no criminal history, hence the applicant may
be enlarged on bail.

the two statements, the role of the applicant that
of catching hold coupled with the fact that is in jail

since 16.8.2023 and has no other criminal history
except one case under the provisions of Wild Life
Protection Act, and there is nothing on record to
demonstrate that the applicant if enlarged on bail,
would in any way adversely affect the trial and
without expressing any opinion on merit, I am of
the view that the applicant is entitled to be
released on bail.

title: BAIL No. 201600001002024 — Allahabad High Court, 17 Dec 2024 (Judge: SUBHASH VIDYARTHI)

paragraphs.text:
Heard Sri Shivam Mishra, learned counsel for the applicant,
Sri Anant Pratap Singh, learned A.G.A. for the State and
perused the records.

Initially the F.I.R. was lodged under Sections 323, 307 I.P.C.
and the applicant was granted bail by means of order dated
29.10.2022, passed by learned Sessions Judge, Raebareli.

Subsequently the victim died on 01.01.2023 i.e. after three
months and 23 days since the incident and thereafter Section
302 I.P.C. was added in the case and the applicant was again
taken into custody.

The learned A.G.A. has opposed the prayer for bail but he
could not dispute the aforesaid aspects of the matter.

Having considered the aforesaid facts and circumstances of
the case and keeping in view the fact that the F.I.r. was lodged
about 24 hours after the incident and it does not make a mention
of the name of any eye witness of the incident and the
informant himself had also not witnessed the incident; that the
victim died after 115 days since the incident due to septicemia;
that all the witnesses of the incident turned hostile; that the
applicant has no previous criminal history and he is languishing
in jail since 23.07.2023 and without making any observation,
which may affect the merits of the case, I am of the view that
the aforesaid facts are sufficient for making out a case for
enlargement of the applicant on bail in the aforesaid crime.
Accordingly, this bail application stands allowed.

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant as well as
learned A.G.A. and perused the record.

In terms of the F.I.R., it was alleged that on 01.08.2023
on account of financial dealing an altercation took place
and the applicant administered some poison through a
tea, which resulted into the death of the husband of the
informant. In the light of the said, the counsel for the
applicant argues that prior to the lodging of FIR, it was
stated by the informant herself that the husband of the
informant had gone to relieve himself, when he was
beaten by a snake and had died on account of snake bite.
He also draws my attention to the inquest report, wherein
prima facie a view was expressed by the Punch that the
death had occurred on account of snake bite.
Subsequently, in the FSL report, the cause of death is
shown as Aluminum Phosphide (poison). In the light of
the said, the submission of the counsel for the applicant is
that apart from the statement of the informant, nothing
exists against the applicant so as to link  to the applicant
with the offence in question. The post mortem report does
not indicate any injury. One of the statement of one
Kamlesh referred to the bail rejection order wherein victim
had stated that brother of the deceased had himself
informed him that the applicant had administered any
poisonous substance through a tea, based upon the said
statement, the applicant is in custody since 13.10.2023.
Learned A.G.A. opposed the bail prayer.

Considering the allegations leveled by the informant
prior to lodging of the FIR, the opinion expressed in the
Punch report, no allegation was levelved against the
applicant, the administering of Aluminum Phosphide
through a tea is prima facie not much trustworthy, there is
no evidence of either a tea stall owner or any passerby to
support the prosecution story, the applicant has no
criminal history and there is nothing on record to
demonstrate that the applicant if enlarged on bail, would
in any way adversely affect the trial and without
expressing any opinion on merit, I am of the view that the
applicant is entitled to be released on bail. Accordingly,
the bail application is allowed.

title: BAIL No. 201600000712024 — Allahabad High Court, 09 Jan 2024 (Judge: PANKAJ BHATIA)

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant, Sri Lalji
Yadav,
 
learned
 
counsel
 
for
 
the
complainant/informant as well as learned A.G.A.
and perused the record.

In terms of the F.I.R., it was alleged that the
daughter of the informant had enticed away by
one Dablu Sahu and a call has also been made
from a particular number by the said person
demanding Rs.10,000/-. Subsequently, however, in
the statement under Section 161 Cr.P.C. the victim 
stated that she was aged about 16 years and she
had gone to her maternal uncle's home at
Pratapgarh, where one Golu and applicant had
taken her by use of force to Prayagraj and
thereafter wrong was done to her. In the statement
under Section 164 Cr.P.C., she stated that she had
gone to see a fair when on the way back one
Devendra and the applicant took her by use of
force to Allahabad in a Car and committed wrong
on her. It was also stated that both of them took
her to Rajasthan thereafter and sold her to a man.
It was also stated that at Allahabad they have
misbehaved with her. It was also stated that there
was a dispute going on in between Imam, the
applicant and Devendra and there were enmity
between the two families. She also stated that
video was also made. In the light of the said, the

submission of the counsel for the applicant is that
in the recovery memo, the police had recovered
the girl from Pratapgarh Bus Stand, thus the entire
story looses the credibility. My attention is also
drawn to the statement of the informant, wherein
he has stated that there was a dispute with regard
to elections to the post of Pradhan with Imamuddin
and the applicant and Devendra used to help him.
In short, apart from the statement under Sections
161 & 164 Cr.P.C., prima facie, no material exists
to corroborate or link the applicant with the
offence in question. The statement under Section
164 Cr.P..C, looses credibility in view of the
recovery memo.
Learned A.G.A. opposed the bail prayer.

Considering the said statements coupled with
the fact that the applicant has no criminal history
and is in jail since 16.08.2023 and there is nothing
on record to demonstrate that the applicant if
enlarged on bail, would in any way adversely
affect the trial and without expressing any opinion
on merit, I am of the view that the applicant is
entitled to be released on bail. Accordingly, the
bail application is allowed.

title: BAIL No. 201600000732024 — Allahabad High Court, 05 Sep 2024 (Judge: PANKAJ BHATIA)

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant, learned AGA and
perused the record.

The accused-applicant seeks bail in Case Crime No.192 of
2023 under section 8/20 NDPS Act, P.S.  Bazar Shukul, District
Amethi.

Learned AGA, on the other hand, strongly opposes the bail
application by arguing that the recovery is more than than the
commercial quantity and thus, in view of the bar prescribed
under Section 37 NDPS Act, the bail applications deserve to be
rejected. He, however, admits that the applicant has no criminal
history of an offence under the NDPS Act.

Considering the submissions made at the Bar, it is clear that
the alleged recovery is more than commercial quantity and the
test of Section 37 of NDPS Act has to be satisfied. The scope of
Section 37 of NDPS Act came up for consideration before the
Supreme Court in Mohd Muslim @ Hussain v. State (NCT of
Delhi); 2023 LiveLaw (SC) 260 wherein, interpreting Section
37, the Supreme Court has observed as under: 
"18. The conditions which courts have to be cognizant of are
that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused
is "not guilty of such offence" and that he is not likely to
commit any offence while on bail. What is meant by "not guilty"
when all the evidence is not before the court? It can only be a
prima facie determination. That places the court's discretion
within a very narrow margin. Given the mandate of the general
law on bails (Sections 436, 437 and 439, CrPC) which classify
offences based on their gravity, and instruct that certain serious
crimes have to be dealt with differently while considering bail
applications, the additional condition that the court should be
satisfied that the accused (who is in law presumed to be
innocent) is not guilty, has to be interpreted reasonably.
Further the classification of offences under Special Acts (NDPS
Act, etc.), which apply over and above the ordinary bail
conditions required to be assessed by courts, require that the
court records its satisfaction that the accused might not be
guilty of the offence and that upon release, they are not likely to
commit any offence. These two conditions have the effect of
overshadowing other conditions. In cases where bail is sought,
the court assesses the material on record such as the nature of
the offence, likelihood of the accused co-operating with the
investigation, not fleeing from justice: even in serious offences
like murder, kidnapping, rape, etc. On the other hand, the court
in these cases under such special Acts, have to address itself
principally on two facts: likely guilt of the accused and the
likelihood of them not committing any offence upon release.
This court has generally upheld such conditions on the ground
that liberty of such citizens have to - in cases when accused of
offences enacted under special laws – be balanced against the
public interest.

Thus based upon these infirmities as recorded above and the
fact that not even a single witness has been examined, the
applicant who is in custody since 25.08.2023 and has no
criminal history of an offence under the NDPS Act, he is
entitled for the bail. The bail application is allowed.

Let the applicant Mohammed Suhaib be released on bail in
aforesaid first information report number subject to his
furnishing a personal bond and two reliable sureties each of the
like amount to the satisfaction of the court concerned with the
following conditions:  
(a) The applicant shall execute a bond to undertake to attend the
hearings;
(b) The applicant shall not commit any offence similar to the
offence of which he is accused or suspected of the commission;
and
(c) The applicant shall not directly or indirectly make any
inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the
facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such
facts to the Court or to any police officer or tamper with the
evidence.

title: BAIL No. 201600000702024 — Allahabad High Court, 02 Jul 2024 (Judge: PANKAJ BHATIA)

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant as
well as learned A.G.A. and perused the record.

Learned counsel for the applicant argued that
in the statement under Section 161 Cr.P.C., the
victim did not support the prosecution story rather
she stated that she had gone alongwith the
applicant on her own free will and they they had
also married.

Learned counsel for the applicant has further
argued that there is no definite document with
regard to the age of the victim which can be
ascertained at the time of trial under the  Juvenile
Justice Act readwith the rules framed thereunder.
The applicant has no criminal history and is in jail
since 18.7.2023, hence the applicant may be
enlarged on bail.

Learned A.G.A. also opposed the prayer for
bail.

Considering the fact that the tentative age of
the victim is around 18 years and the statement of
the victim recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C.
which does not corroborate the prosecution story
coupled with the fact that the applicant has no
criminal history and is languishing in jail since
18.7.2023; and without expressing any opinion on
merit, I am of the view that the applicant is

entitled to be released on bail.
Accordingly, the bail application is allowed.

Heard learned counsel for the applicant as well

supported by any material evidence whatsoever,
the applicant has no criminal history and is in
custody since 11.10.2023 and there is nothing on
record to demonstrate that the applicant if
enlarged on bail, would in any way adversely
affect the trial and without expressing any opinion
on merit, I am of the view that the applicant is
entitled to be released on bail. Accordingly, the
bail application is allowed.

title: BAIL No. 201600000322024 — Allahabad High Court, 10 May 2024 (Judge: PANKAJ BHATIA)

paragraphs.text:
Heard learned counsel for the applicant as
well as Shri Shani Pratap Singh, learned A.G.A. and
perused the record.

Learned counsel for the applicant has drawn
my attention to the medical report on record
including the radiological examination where the
age of the victim was assessed at around 15
years.  The medical report with respect to internal
examination done on 4.9.2023 does not indicate
any injury present on the external or internal part
of the victim.   He further drawn my attention to
the statement of the independent witnesses who
stated that on account of payment with regard to
certain crops, there existed an enmity in between
the family of the informant and the applicant.  The

independent witness has also stated that on the
said date, he has seen both the daughters of the
informant present on the spot including the elder
sister of the victim.

Learned A.G.A. however opposed the prayer
for bail by arguing that the age of the victim is less
than 18 years and considering the gravity of the
allegations, the bail application should be rejected.

Considering the statements of the independent
witnesses  coupled with the fact that there is
inordinate delay in lodging the F.I.R. without there
being any explanation, the applicant who is in
custody since 7.9.2023 having no criminal history 
and there is nothing on record to demonstrate that
the applicant if enlarged on bail, would in any way
adversely affect the trial and without expressing
any opinion on merit, I am of the view that the
applicant is entitled to be released on bail.
Accordingly, the bail application is allowed.

title: BAIL No. 201600000292024 — Allahabad High Court, 17 Jan 2024 (Judge: MOHD. FAIZ ALAM KHAN)

paragraphs.text:
Learned AGA informs that he has procured complete
instructions in the matter including upto date case diary  and the
charge sheet in this case so far as the applicant is concerned has
already been submitted.

Heard Shri Anil Kumar Yadav, learned counsel for the
accused/applicant, Shri Amitav Singh, learned counsel for the
complainant/ informant as well as learned A.G.A. for the State
and perused the record.

Learned counsel for the accused-applicant while pressing the
bail application submits that it is a case of false implication.
The applicant has not committed any misappropriation  of the
money as shown in the FIR and in the statement of the
prosecution witnesses.

Elaborating further, it is submitted that it appears that some
misappropriation of money  earmarked to be  deposited in the

A.T.Ms. have been misappropriated and in order to conceal the
real culprit  the soft targets have been alleged as accused
persons including the applicant.

It is further submitted that except the presence of the
applicant in various A.T.Ms. which have been found in the
CCTV Footage there is no evidence with regard to the
commission of the offence and the presence of the applicant in
various ATMs is natural,  so far as his duties are concerned.

It is further submitted that criminal history of one case has
been explained in paragraph 11 of the supplementary affidavit,
however, the same is with regard to the personal dispute and is
not connected with  any misappropriated money or fraud etc.
